figures.caption: Table 2: Support generalization (pass@k). Evaluating the interpolation vs. extrapolation gap across five independent runs. While evaluating on out-of-support functional behaviors (semantic manifold) incurs virtually no relative penalty, extrapolating to out-of-support syntactic structures causes significant performance degradation.

Figure 3: Scaling laws for generalization. Performance (pass@1) as a function of compute (FLOPs). (a–c) Density Generalization: All models exhibit strictly log-linear improvements regardless of the sampling strategy. (d–e) Support Generalization: Semantic extrapolation (d) scales identically to interpolation, whereas structural extrapolation (e) suffers a persistent OOD penalty that cannot be easily overcome by simply scaling up compute.

Figure 4: Visualizing density generalization splits. Projection of the Diverse, Semantic, and Syntactic datasets onto the semantic (top) and syntactic (bottom) manifolds. The scatter plots (a) illustrate the spatial coverage of the respective sampling strategies. The histograms (b) display the local density, measured as the average distance to the 5-nearest neighbors. Inverse-density sampling (red) successfully flattens the distribution compared to the naturally center-dense Diverse sampling (blue), forcing the training data to cover sparser, more isolated regions of the manifolds.

Figure 5: Visualizing support generalization splits. Geometric partitioning of the program space into interpolation and extrapolation regimes. The scatter plots (a) show the distribution of the splits within the semantic (top) and syntactic (bottom) manifolds. The histograms (b) plot the eccentricity (Euclidean distance to the manifold centroid). A strict radius threshold successfully isolates the training and interpolation sets (inner region) from the strictly out-of-distribution extrapolation set (outer region).

Figure 16: Scaling laws for generalization. Performance (pass@1) as a function of compute (FLOPs). (a–c) Density generalization: Allmodels exhibit strictly log-linear improvements regardless of the sampling strategy. (d–e) Support generalization: Semantic extrapolation (d) scales identically to interpolation, whereas structural extrapolation (e) suffers a persistent OOD penalty that cannot be easily overcome by simply scaling up compute.

Figure 19: Support generalization across scales. Interpolation versus extrapolation performance across semantic (top) and syntactic (bottom) manifolds. The structural extrapolation penalty (shaded area, bottom row) remains severe andwidens with increased scale and sampling budgets, confirming that test-time scaling cannot overcome the model’s limitations to synthesize unseen syntactic structures.

Figure 18: Density generalization across scales. Performance (pass@k) of models evaluated across data distributions as a function of compute. Because removing semantic ambiguity makes the synthesis task vastly more difficult, absolute accuracy is drastically reduced compared to the main experiment. However, the fundamental log-linear scaling dynamics and the relative robustness of the Diverse training strategy remain entirely consistent.

Figure 17: Distance to nearest training neighbor. Comparing distance of solved (blue) vs. failed (black) test instances across semantic (top) and syntactic (bottom) manifolds. When evaluated out-of-distribution (panels b and c), models successfully solve instances that are significantly closer to their pre-training support, indicating a reliance on local manifold interpolation.

Figure 1: Dual manifold projection pipeline. To formally quantify out-of-distribution distances, arithmetic programs are embedded into two continuous spaces. In the syntactic pipeline, code is parsed into an AST, represented as a sparse vector of PQ-Grams, and condensed using a linear projection (SVD). In the semantic pipeline, the program’s functional behavior is evaluated over a fixed input grid, z-score standardized, and also reduced via a linear projection (PCA).

Figure 9: Density generalization across model and test-time scales. Performance (pass@1, pass@5, pass@10) of models trained on Diverse, Semantic, and Syntactic distributions, evaluated across corresponding test splits as a function of compute (FLOPs). Increasing the sample budget 𝑘 (test-time scaling) shifts absolute performance upwards while strictly maintaining the underlying log-linear scaling dynamics. The Diverse training strategy (blue) remains consistently robust across all out-of-distribution shifts regardless of the sampling budget.

Figure 10: Support generalization across model and test-time scales. Interpolation (solid) versus extrapolation (dashed) performance across semantic (top) and syntactic (bottom) manifolds for pass@1, pass@5, and pass@10. While increasing the test-time sampling budget 𝑘 improves absolute accuracy, it completely fails to close the persistent out-of-distribution gap (shaded area) on the syntactic manifold. Conversely, semantic extrapolation remains tightly coupled with interpolation across all scales and budgets.

Figure 2: Characterizing the growth behavior of the arithmetic program space. A comparison of syntactic versus semantic growth as a function of program length (number of operations). The total number of syntactically valid programs grows exponentially, far outpacing the growth in the number of unique semantic behaviors (equivalency classes). This demonstrates a high degree of redundancy within the language.

Figure 23: Manifold approximation (2D Example). (a) Training coverage: A top-down view showing dense training data in the center. The interpolation zone covers the area where data density is high,making successful synthesis highly probable (green star). (b) Manifold divergence: A 3D view showing the model’s learned flat plane (red grid) approximating the true non-linear data manifold (gray surface) locally. In the center, the approximation is highly accurate. However, as one moves into the extrapolation zone, the true manifold curves upward while themodel’s learned approximation continues linearly, causing a massive divergence that results in generalization failure (red cross).

Figure 14: Visualizing support generalization splits. Geometric partitioning of the semantically unique program space. The scatter plots (a) and eccentricity histograms (b) demonstrate the strict spatial separation of the interpolation regime (inner radius) from the pure extrapolation regime (outer radius) across both the semantic and syntactic manifolds.

Figure 13: Visualizing density generalization splits. Projection of the Diverse, Semantic, and Syntactic datasets onto the continuous manifolds for the strictly deduplicated dataset. The scatter plots (a) and local density histograms (b) confirm that inverse-density sampling (red) successfully targets sparse regions and flattens the density distribution, even after all semantic redundancies have been removed from the search space.

Figure 8: Multi-modal transformer architecture. Inspired by vision-language models, we bypass standard byte-pair encoding (BPE) for the numerical inputs to prevent tokenization artifacts. Instead, continuous input-output execution pairs are processed by a point encoder and linearly projected directly into the transformer’s continuous embedding space. The decoder then autoregressively generates the corresponding sequence of discrete arithmetic program tokens.

Figure 7: Nearest neighbors in the semantic manifold. This figure illustrates a query program’s output (thick gray) alongside its three nearest neighbors (N1, N2, N3) in the continuous semantic embedding space. Closeness in this manifold corresponds to highly correlated functional behaviors (Pearson’s 𝑟 ≥ 0.99). As shown, the embedding successfully captures the overarching shape of the mathematical function, even if the individual programs exhibit minor local phase or amplitude variations.
